turn_text: Great. And, you know, let's talk a little bit more about what that process is actually like. When you were in Congress, you were a member of the Republican Party. I mentioned this nearby, but there were several times where you took stands at the time, at least, when popular with their party on things like climate policy, to name one instance. What is that process actually like behind the scenes when you are in a position of leadership? Do none of the other members of Congress sit with you at the cafeteria as a result of it? Is there more acceptance of it behind the scenes? And fundamentally, why do you think we don't see more members of Congress taking these sorts of stands?

Look, Gil, it's in almost everything in life. It's easier to get along just by going along. So if you're sitting with 20 of your Republican friends and 19 of them say, hey, for example, This whole climate change discussion is a hoax. This whole idea about carbon dioxide emissions contributing to global warming. That's just fake and made up. Many times the easy thing to do is to either ignore it or say, oh, yeah, that's true. Maybe laugh it off. It's far more difficult to intervene and say, well, actually, I disagree. This is why. And this is why we should be thinking differently, especially acting differently when it comes to this. So I found myself a lot of times of swimming against the current, going against the grain. taking extraordinary actions to force important discussions and debates. We certainly did that on immigration. You mentioned in my bio that we let a discharge petition process. That's all technical and complicated. And we don't have to explain the whole thing here today, but essentially it forced Republicans to have an honest intra party debate and discussion about immigration and members learn and a lot of preconceived notions were dispelled and people understood better why a lot of these DACA recipients. It just makes all the sense in the world for them to be American citizens because they've been here since they're two, three, four, five years old and grew up here and speak better English than some people who were born here. So I found myself in that position many times, but look, I don't want to only focus on where Republicans can improve, but You know, Democrats have a similar challenge. For example, I was excluded from the congressional Hispanic caucus by Democrats because I didn't agree with them on every issue because I was a Republican. They essentially said, no, you're not Hispanic because you're not a Democrat. So I wasn't allowed to join a caucus that was formed to include all Hispanics serving in Congress. And that kind of Attitude and mentality is also destructive, right? Where we just kind of shut out anyone who who doesn't fully agree with us. That's not What our founders had in mind when they developed a government that was that's designed to operate based on consensus, right? You have a house a Senate They both have to pass bills in the Senate the threshold is higher for a lot of bills and you have an executive that has to sign the bill then you have a court system that can review legislation so We're really designed to sit at a table, bring our disagreements to that table, have a negotiation, give some, take some, and then move forward in a way where everyone gets something in the country and our communities are better off. That's not happening now. And I think that this rising generation of leaders, business, civic, political leaders, has to not only be committed to the truth, but also has to be committed to civil discourse and dialogue, using facts, using data, not disqualifying people just because they disagree. These are all things that probably our parents and grandparents taught us, but that a lot of adults in our society are not following, and the victims could be the people who inherit this country. So all of you who are listening today, so it's important that all of us and all of you be a part of the solution and not make things worse.
